item.text: {"chapter_id":"2B","answers":[{"question_id":"2B.1","answer":"Tshisekedi repeatedly used formal diplomatic and regional channels before and alongside force: he convened FARDC, MONUSCO, and EAC officials to implement the Luanda process, pursued Nairobi and Luanda mechanisms, supported ceasefire and withdrawal plans, and called for M23 disarmament and cantonment (BATCH-0021-E001; BATCH-0021-E003; BATCH-0027-E010; BATCH-0027-E013). He also authorized or supported regional-force cooperation and humanitarian/security coordination, while inviting a national review of the state of siege and proposing peaceful demobilization through P-DDRCS (BATCH-0007-E002; BATCH-0007-E003; BATCH-0021-E012). However, the record is mixed: his government rejected political dialogue with M23, adopted a hardline position, and continued military mobilization while negotiations and ceasefires repeatedly failed or produced limited results (BATCH-0011-E016; BATCH-0011-E017; BATCH-0007-E013; BATCH-0027-E006). The evidence establishes formal initiatives and stated alternatives, but implementation, sincerity of some negotiations, and whether more credible alternatives existed are uncertain.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0021-E001","BATCH-0021-E003","BATCH-0027-E010","BATCH-0027-E013","BATCH-0007-E002","BATCH-0007-E003"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0011-E016","BATCH-0011-E017","BATCH-0007-E013","BATCH-0027-E006"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index does not provide complete cabinet or parliamentary deliberations, classified operational records, or a definitive counterfactual showing which peaceful alternatives were feasible.","Many positive accounts are official statements or plans without verified implementation outcomes."]},{"question_id":"2B.2","answer":"The strongest evidence concerns defensive or inherited conflict rather than a clearly documented war of choice: M23 and ADF violence, alleged Rwandan intervention, mass displacement, and loss of territorial control created a substantial security threat (BATCH-0016-E004; BATCH-0029-E009; BATCH-0006-E002; BATCH-0010-E003). Tshisekedi authorized continued FARDC operations, cooperation with Uganda and regional forces, recruitment, an armed reserve, and support for Wazalendo and other armed partners; his government also retained the state of siege and contracted private military personnel (BATCH-0010-E008; BATCH-0028-E016; BATCH-0011-E019). These measures were presented as defensive, but the use of irregular partners, hardline rhetoric, refusal of dialogue with M23, and failed or ended regional-force deployments created escalation and proxy-risk concerns (BATCH-0011-E017; BATCH-0011-E016; BATCH-0027-E006). The record does not establish that Tshisekedi initiated an unlawful interstate war or annexation, but it does document expansion and entrenchment of militarized policy beyond clearly demonstrated defensive necessity in some areas.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0016-E004","BATCH-0029-E009","BATCH-0006-E002","BATCH-0010-E008"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0028-E016","BATCH-0011-E019","BATCH-0011-E017","BATCH-0011-E016","BATCH-0027-E006"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index lacks complete operational orders, force-composition data, spending records, and independent findings on whether specific cross-border operations exceeded defensive necessity.","Attribution for many battlefield actions remains institutional rather than personal."]},{"question_id":"2B.3","answer":"Tshisekedi consistently presented the conflict as external aggression, especially alleged Rwandan support for M23, and supplied memoranda or diplomatic appeals to the UN, AU, and international partners; UN experts and Western governments provided some corroboration for Rwandan support, although Rwanda denied the allegations (BATCH-0006-E011; BATCH-0021-E006; BATCH-0014-E001; BATCH-0029-E009). He also stated concrete objectives such as M23 withdrawal, return of displaced people, sanctions, regional diplomacy, and restoration of sovereignty (BATCH-0016-E002; BATCH-0004-E001; BATCH-0007-E008). Conversely, campaign and wartime rhetoric described opponents and Rwanda in highly adversarial terms, urged mass enlistment, and used claims not independently verified in the record, including recruitment totals and some allegations of foreign manipulation (BATCH-0007-E013; BATCH-0018-E007; BATCH-0019-E011). Thus, the evidence shows a reviewable external-threat narrative with partial independent support, but also selective, partisan, and potentially escalatory presentation; the index does not establish deliberate fabrication.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0006-E011","BATCH-0021-E006","BATCH-0014-E001","BATCH-0016-E002","BATCH-0004-E001"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0007-E013","BATCH-0018-E007","BATCH-0019-E011","BATCH-0029-E009"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index does not contain full intelligence assessments, cabinet records, or independent verification of every public claim.","Evidence of motive, diversionary politics, or deliberate threat manufacture is inferential rather than directly established."]},{"question_id":"2B.4","answer":"The government adopted formal safeguards and accountability mechanisms, including victim-reparation legislation, military codes and commander commitments, specialized training, investigations, prosecutions, and cooperation with the ICC (BATCH-0029-E001; BATCH-0029-E002; BATCH-0011-E003; BATCH-0011-E004; BATCH-0019-E001). Some security personnel were prosecuted or convicted, including after the Goma operation, and the government announced investigations into abuses (BATCH-0011-E018; BATCH-0011-E021; BATCH-0023-E014; BATCH-0002-E012). Implementation was materially adverse: UN and rights monitors documented killings, sexual violence, arbitrary detention, child recruitment, and other abuses by state forces and armed groups; Goma casualty figures were disputed, investigations were incomplete, and military authorities used force against civilians under a prolonged state of siege (BATCH-0011-E009; BATCH-0010-E015; BATCH-0011-E020; BATCH-0009-E002). The conduct therefore combines formal legal commitments and selective enforcement with serious operational failures and uncertain remedy.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0029-E001","BATCH-0029-E002","BATCH-0011-E003","BATCH-0011-E004","BATCH-0019-E001","BATCH-0011-E018","BATCH-0011-E021"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0011-E009","BATCH-0010-E015","BATCH-0011-E020","BATCH-0009-E002","BATCH-0023-E014"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index does not provide complete rules of engagement, operational logs, or independent audits of command enforcement.","Many abuses are attributed to state institutions or armed groups rather than personally to Tshisekedi."]},{"question_id":"2B.5","answer":"Tshisekedi’s government established or supported regional-force arrangements, joint operations with Uganda, P-DDRCS, Wazalendo mobilization, and an Armed Defence Reserve, while publicly linking these arrangements to security and civilian protection (BATCH-0010-E008; BATCH-0006-E001; BATCH-0007-E003; BATCH-0011-E019). There were also some formal disarmament, monitoring, and rules-of-engagement frameworks through the Nairobi and EAC processes (BATCH-0028-E008; BATCH-0027-E013; BATCH-0028-E013). The adverse record is substantial: the army supported or fought alongside non-state groups, surrendered fighters were transferred for military training without adequate vetting, and rights organizations reported support for Wazalendo and FDLR despite foreseeable abuse and escalation risks (BATCH-0010-E015; BATCH-0028-E016; BATCH-0012-R04-E004). The EAC force failed to achieve expected results and was withdrawn, while no complete evidence shows systematic monitoring, suspension of abusive partners, or effective correction.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0010-E008","BATCH-0006-E001","BATCH-0007-E003","BATCH-0028-E008","BATCH-0027-E013","BATCH-0028-E013"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0010-E015","BATCH-0028-E016","BATCH-0012-R04-E004","BATCH-0011-E016","BATCH-0011-E017"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index lacks arms-transfer contracts, partner vetting files, monitoring reports, and evidence of presidential knowledge of specific proxy abuses.","Some allegations concern earlier or imprecisely dated support and cannot be confined to 2023."]},{"question_id":"2B.6","answer":"Tshisekedi and his government permitted some external and domestic scrutiny: CENI announced mixed external audits, invited election observers, cooperated with the ICC, received AU and UN delegations, and allowed some human-rights monitoring and National Commission reporting (BATCH-0027-E011; BATCH-0028-E007; BATCH-0019-E001; BATCH-0021-E006; BATCH-0011-E014). He also convened a public roundtable to review the state of siege and made some public acknowledgments of institutional and justice-system problems (BATCH-0021-E012; BATCH-0028-E017). However, authorities restricted or narrowed scrutiny: the EU mission was reduced or canceled after equipment authorization problems, CENI did not fully disclose or independently audit the register, UN access to some detention facilities was denied, journalists were arrested or attacked, and election tabulation and irregularities remained contested (BATCH-0028-E003; BATCH-0013-E009; BATCH-0011-E014; BATCH-0019-E013; BATCH-0028-E022). The record shows partial openness combined with significant obstruction and no clear correction of misleading or disputed official accounts.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0027-E011","BATCH-0028-E007","BATCH-0019-E001","BATCH-0021-E006","BATCH-0021-E012"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0028-E003","BATCH-0013-E009","BATCH-0011-E014","BATCH-0019-E013","BATCH-0028-E022"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Most restrictions are attributed to CENI, security agencies, or authorities collectively rather than directly to Tshisekedi.","The index does not establish whether the president personally reviewed or rejected specific independent findings."]},{"question_id":"2B.7","answer":"Tshisekedi’s government participated in the Nairobi and Luanda processes, supported ceasefire and withdrawal mechanisms, pursued regional-force arrangements, called for M23 cantonment and disarmament, and signed a formal MONUSCO disengagement plan (BATCH-0027-E010; BATCH-0027-E013; BATCH-0021-E001; BATCH-0010-E007). Some ceasefires broadly held for periods, and the government periodically sought diplomacy, humanitarian access, and international mediation (BATCH-0018-E002; BATCH-0023-E010; BATCH-0015-E002). Durability was weak: M23 did not fully withdraw, dialogue with M23 was rejected, ceasefires broke down in October, the EAC mandate ended without measurable security improvement, and displacement and fighting increased late in 2023 (BATCH-0004-E001; BATCH-0011-E017; BATCH-0027-E006; BATCH-0011-E016; BATCH-0013-E014). The evidence supports genuine but inconsistent peace-process engagement, with limited implementation and no durable settlement by the end of the period.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0027-E010","BATCH-0027-E013","BATCH-0021-E001","BATCH-0010-E007","BATCH-0018-E002","BATCH-0015-E002"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0004-E001","BATCH-0011-E017","BATCH-0027-E006","BATCH-0011-E016","BATCH-0013-E014"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index does not provide complete compliance records for each party or establish which failures were within Tshisekedi’s control.","The MONUSCO withdrawal plan was formalized late in the period, so durable effects were not yet observable."]},{"question_id":"2B.8","answer":"The government framed military mobilization and reform as responses to M23, ADF, territorial insecurity, and the need to protect civilians; Tshisekedi issued military directives, supported army reform, regional operations, recruitment, and force-capacity measures (BATCH-0019-E010; BATCH-0022-E003; BATCH-0010-E008; BATCH-0006-E001). There were formal budgeting, procurement, and monitoring frameworks in the wider government, but the index supplies little conflict-specific expenditure transparency or proportionality evidence (BATCH-0017-E005; BATCH-0029-E005; BATCH-0020-E011). Adverse evidence includes prolonged militarization, private military contracting, armed-drone acquisition, support for irregular forces, and a security strategy whose results were mixed while displacement and violence remained high (BATCH-0028-E016; BATCH-0011-E019; BATCH-0012-R07-E003; BATCH-0010-E003). The record supports genuine security needs but cannot show that budgets and procurement were consistently transparent, proportionate, or free from network entrenchment.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0019-E010","BATCH-0022-E003","BATCH-0010-E008","BATCH-0006-E001","BATCH-0017-E005","BATCH-0029-E005"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0028-E016","BATCH-0011-E019","BATCH-0012-R07-E003","BATCH-0010-E003"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The candidate index lacks defense-budget line items, procurement audits, contract beneficiaries, and reliable comparisons with threat levels.","Military outcomes are heavily affected by armed groups, Rwanda, regional forces, and inherited institutional weakness."]},{"question_id":"2B.9","answer":"The government sought external accountability through ICC referrals, a cooperation agreement with the ICC prosecutor, UN and AU engagement, calls for sanctions, and some domestic prosecutions and investigations (BATCH-0005-E001; BATCH-0019-E001; BATCH-0019-E002; BATCH-0015-E003; BATCH-0011-E002). It also enacted victim-reparation and protection laws and announced investigations into security-force abuses, including the Goma operation (BATCH-0029-E001; BATCH-0029-E002; BATCH-0023-E014). Conversely, transitional-justice commitments lacked concrete implementation, many atrocities remained unpunished, investigations were incomplete or contested, families lacked information and remedy, and authorities denied some independent access (BATCH-0010-E016; BATCH-0011-E020; BATCH-0028-E018; BATCH-0011-E014). Tshisekedi sometimes acknowledged justice failures and publicly claimed non-intervention in an individual case, but the record does not demonstrate consistent responsibility-taking, discipline of senior actors, or effective reparations.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0005-E001","BATCH-0019-E001","BATCH-0019-E002","BATCH-0015-E003","BATCH-0029-E001","BATCH-0029-E002","BATCH-0023-E014"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0010-E016","BATCH-0011-E020","BATCH-0028-E018","BATCH-0011-E014","BATCH-0025-E013"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index does not contain final outcomes for several investigations, ICC processes, or reparations mechanisms.","Presidential responsibility for individual prosecutorial or military decisions is often not established."]},{"question_id":"2B.10","answer":"Tshisekedi inherited a long-running eastern conflict involving more than 100 armed groups, external intervention, weak state presence, and mass displacement; some diplomatic, regional, humanitarian, and transition institutions were maintained or created during 2023 (BATCH-0012-R04-E001; BATCH-0010-E015; BATCH-0010-E007; BATCH-0021-E001). He pursued peace processes, regional cooperation, P-DDRCS, ceasefire implementation, and a planned MONUSCO transition, and conflict-related violations documented by UNJHRO declined relative to 2022, though reporting and conflict composition may explain part of that decline (BATCH-0027-E010; BATCH-0027-E013; BATCH-0025-E009). The end state nevertheless remained severely adverse: M23 expanded or retained territory, fighting and displacement rose late in 2023, millions remained displaced, ceasefires failed, and the EAC force withdrew without measurable security improvement (BATCH-0013-E014; BATCH-0028-E016; BATCH-0011-E016; BATCH-0010-E003). The evidence supports partial diplomatic and institutional effort but not a demonstrated transition to more peaceful, stable, or lawful international relations by period-end.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0012-R04-E001","BATCH-0010-E015","BATCH-0010-E007","BATCH-0021-E001","BATCH-0027-E010","BATCH-0027-E013","BATCH-0025-E009"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0013-E014","BATCH-0028-E016","BATCH-0011-E016","BATCH-0010-E003","BATCH-0027-E006"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The period ends amid active conflict, so durable institutional and settlement effects cannot yet be measured.","Causal attribution is constrained by inherited conflict, armed-group agency, neighboring-state involvement, regional-force limits, and humanitarian funding constraints."]}],"cross_lens_observations":[]}
